cards.title: Show HN: Reladraw – A diagram language where you decide where to place things

depth.text: someone made **Reladraw**, a diagram language where you choose **where things go**

The author wanted a middle ground between auto-placement tools like **Mermaid and Graphviz** and **Draw.io**, which is powerful but time-consuming and inefficient for agents. Reladraw lets you define diagrams in a language while keeping **control over how they look**; there's a playground, npm install instructions, and a skill for Claude or other agents.

comments.text: This is very needed in the AI coding age! I find diagramming is one of the best ways for high bandwidth alignment between my mental model and the agent’s. I have been working on this problem a bit as I see good visuals as a key bottleneck in faster development while maintaining a real architecture. Will def be adding this to my list of diagramming tools the agent can use!
The README looks LLM generated. Sorry, but that's where my interaction stops

Mermaid works great for fixed layouts like sequence diagrams and Gantts. For flowcharts, where position is king, it's bad. I've tried using svg in my MD files but they get unwieldy quite fast. This is a great idea. My first reaction was - but what's if I need something more exact. But reflecting on it, I've realized that this relative positioning is probably enough.
OP, is this something I could use when someone is explaining their architecture and this simply can interpret their words into a diagram?

cards.title: Does Georgism work? Five years later

depth.text: someone looks back at **Georgism** and says its advocates need to focus on **practical policy work**

Lars Doucet says Virginia and Kentucky passed laws allowing municipalities to **tax land more and buildings less**. His group built maps of local land values and published a **policy playbook**; a Louisville activist used it to get a bill passed in his state legislature.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters say LVT is fair and can tackle rent-seeking; skeptics question whether Georgism has worked before, whether land supply is really fixed, and whether it would improve housing without just raising taxes.

comments.text: I’ve since learned that overly online keyboard warriors are the least important people to convince. The most important people are on your local city council or state legislature. Furthermore, instead of wasting time with hard cases or elected officials who are dead-set against your ideas, you’re much better off finding and working with people who are already interested in your principles. This…

It's freakishly weird to see this at the top of HN. I had never heard or read anything about Georgism until last week, when I stumbled onto it after randomly seeing a photo of a 100-year-old billboard on the Wikipedia page for the term "speculation". I spent a few days researching it on and off. In fact, I just navigated to HN from the last page I was reading about it. It seems like a clever way…

I think LVT does have a history in US, e.g Pittsburgh. Also Georgism is 100% LVT -> A land tax alone has been the recommendation of many economists before and after George - From Smith, Riccardo, Mill to Friedman. Across classical, neoclassical, Keynesian, Austrian schools. If there's one thing economists can agree on, it's that land tax is better than income tax.

"Doing policymaker's work for them" is something like 80% of lobbying. If you have something you want done in your town, and you come with the work done AND not asking for funding, you're likely to get it. If you come with the work done and a PLAN for getting the funding, you also have a good chance of success.

There's a lot here to absorb, but one thing I've always wondered about Georgism and Land Value Tax is whether land supply is actually inelastic: > Land, however, is not built. Land is inelastic in supply, and landowners don’t “provide” land the way laborers provide labor and investors provide capital; they un-provide land by excluding others from using it. Building supply can change in response…

depth.text: DeepSeek built a system that spins up and manages huge numbers of **sandboxes** for **AI training**

It exposes **FnCall, container, microVM and full-VM backends** through a unified SDK, and handles placement, sandbox lifecycles, memory sharing and CPU scheduling. cards.title: How to keep enjoying programming in a world of LLMs

depth.text: someone says to **keep writing code** yourself and let LLMs handle the **boring work** around it

The author, a Haskell programmer, suggests using LLMs to turn expert conversations into todos, organize test results, and research the codebase. Keep the decisions and most coding human-led, save research with links, and use an **automated review cycle** for plans and generated code.

cards.camps: Two camps: some want to keep coding by hand to protect their skills and enjoyment; others say LLMs take away grunt work and leave energy for interesting problems.

After every assignment, each student schedules a **15-minute meeting with a TA** to answer a couple of questions in a **live conversation**.

depth.text: someone made a **hands-on** **Go concurrency** refresher, with examples you can change and run yourself
It gets into **channel patterns** for pipelines and cancellation, plus error handling, timers, contexts, data races, the race detector, **mutexes**, and semaphores.

comments.text: The concurrency and threading in Go just feels like magic compared to every other language. I'm a goroutine addict and I refuse to be rehabilitated. Just from observations over the years, I don't think there's any other language quite like this, in terms of how things can end up happening in any thread.

Ive been writing Go for over a decade and I still feel like I never quite "got" channels. Every time I use them I need to go consult the manual, and none of the patterns feel obvious which is weird considering the rest of the language feels very obvious. Too many years of Java and managing Threads and Runnables probably rotted my brain.

One thing I always found more work than I would expect is when you have a graph of operations, think a Makefile, but a bit dynamic. For this model completable futures and executors seem to work well (provided the graphs is smallish), but golang is (or perhaps before generics) just was difficult.

For many people, besides learning what you should do, it is more helpful to read anti-patterns and things you should not do in Go, and none is better than this article about data race patterns in Go: https://www.uber.com/us/en/blog/data-race-patterns-in-go/
honestly the hard part of go concurrency was never starting goroutines, it's making cancellation and shutdown behave. nice to see context, races and diagnostics in one runnable place.

cards.title: What is the size of Yemen? (2024)

depth.text: someone questioned **Yemen's listed size**, and commenters say a **decades-old mistake** was eventually corrected

A commenter says someone found a **“correct looking number”** in a **Yemen government document published in 2005** and updated Wikipedia on 3 December. Another remembered hearing that the border with Saudi was undefined, and wondered if that ambiguity meant sources kept carrying old figures.

comments.text: I think a more important question is whether Yemen still exists as as single coherent political entity with the same borders as seen on ANY of those maps, which given the present situation, it clearly does not. edit: map here https://understandingwar.org/research/middle-east/iran-updat... and here: https://yemen.liveuamap.com/

this was posted on 27. of november 2024. on the 3rd of december someone found a correct looking number in a yemen government document which was published in 2005 and updated wikipedia. so at least the country itself was not under any illusion of being bigger than they actually are.
This reminds me of what Deming used to say: there is no correct value for any measurement, there are only the outcomes of methods chosen to measure something.
What I wonder is why anyone noticed this in the first place. Who saw the size of the country in Wikipedia and thought, “really? Let me trace that in Google maps, just to be sure…”

I remember hearing from a Yemeni American in the late 90s that the border with Saudi was not defined (mentioned in the article). I wonder if this could be explained more simply that a few sources didn't bother to update this over time due to the ambiguity, they just carried over what had been published before.

cards.title: If we do not stop to help each other, what do we become?

depth.text: someone remembers **Stack Overflow strangers** helping during a siege, and worries AI answers can’t replace **human connection**

During the **Zamboanga Siege**, the writer was serving in the Air Force and studying remotely; strangers on Stack Overflow nudged him when he got stuck. He says an LLM could have answered his questions, but not made him feel **somebody cared**, and urges people to build online communities that belong to them.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say Stack Overflow built skills and community; others remember its toxicity and prefer AI for troubleshooting.

comments.text:
Stack overflow was one of the best ways to learn and mature as an engineer “back in the day”. The
meme is that devs would copy and paste and hope it worked. The reality was more like you had an obscure bug, you wrote a detailed and cohesive question, and you connected with people who were more knowledgable and would help you. It also sharpened your writing and thinking. By responding to questions…

Maybe I'm remembering a different Stack Overflow. Yes, there were genuinely helpful people there. I strove to be helpful as well. But my most common experience there was: - People asking why you're doing that (without answering the question). - People telling you that you shouldn't do that (without answering the question or providing an alternative). - People closing your question as off-topic or…

On the GrapheneOS forum, I enjoy answering the questions in a post of user who just set up their phone. AI does not have as good knowledge of the OS as frequent forum contributors. I'm sure plenty of people get by with AI help for their questions and there's likely little questions that hasn't been already discussed, but I love to see new people using the OS and it doesn't take long to give them…

the sense of community on the internet from 1995 to 2010 was incredible. industry devs running into tricky situations and just asking for help on irc, newsgroups like comp.lang.*, then forums, places like expert-sexchange and gamedev.net - the people that helped were like heroes and mentors and the urge to pay it forward was real and strong. stackoverflow was cool when it first launched - then…

We had better have even more time to help each other as a result of LLMs, or what are we even doing here? I realize that everything seems to be about increasing the pace of life, but this is another "chance" for humanity to figure things out.

cards.title: Drawgent: Coding agent on a live Excalidraw canvas

depth.text: someone hooked their **coding agent** up to a **live whiteboard** it can edit alongside them

Drawgent connects your own **Claude Code, Codex or opencode** setup to Excalidraw. The agent looks at the canvas and **edits it live**; `--diagram` can also keep a standard `.excalidraw` file in your repo in sync.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters say live diagrams could help brainstorm or scaffold ideas; skeptics say it may not beat typing and AI-made diagrams still feel like slop.

comments.text: Excalidraw offers their own open source first party MCP endpoint[0] and server[1]: [0] https://mcp.excalidraw.com [1] https://github.com/excalidraw/excalidraw-mcp

To my surprise, current solutions (including Excalidraw) were not good enough and didn't deliver what I wanted. I ended up finding Mermaid to be the most agent-friendly medium and coded an Obsidian plugin for it. It works okay; we can work on the same doc while I bring my own…

YMMV, but the value I get from producing a diagram is derived from the thinking. Thinking about what I'm trying to draw leads to understanding about where my/my team's knowledge is poorer, what assumptions we're making, etc.
Posted this somewhere else aswell but I've had good success with https://whiteboard-mcp.com - it seems to work better than other free alternatives for things like architecture diagram creation

One other option, if you're an obsidian user is, just add the excalidraw plugin there, and then you can ask your agent to just create excalidraw diagrams as needed. Definitely Opus 5.5 via claude code has no problems generating Excalidraw images with no additional software, just based on conversation.

glossary.auto-placement: When a tool chooses where the pieces of a diagram go for you.
glossary.renderer: The part of a tool that turns instructions into the picture you see.
glossary.DSLs: Domain-specific languages: small languages made for describing one particular kind of thing.
glossary.SVG: Scalable Vector Graphics: a picture format that stays sharp when resized.
glossary.npm: A tool people use to add software packages to JavaScript projects.
glossary.Georgism: A view that land's value should be taxed for public benefit, rather than taxing work or investment.
glossary.LVT: Land Value Tax: a tax on the land's value, not on buildings or other improvements on it.
glossary.split-rate property tax: A property tax that taxes land and buildings at different rates, usually taxing land more and buildings less.
glossary.rent-seeking: Making money by controlling something valuable without creating much useful value yourself.
glossary.upzoning: Changing local rules to allow more or larger buildings on a piece of land.
glossary.rent control: Rules that limit how much landlords can charge or how quickly rents can rise.
glossary.single tax: The idea that land rent would be taxed at its full yearly value and that this would be the only tax.
glossary.UBI: Universal Basic Income: money regularly given to people without requiring them to work for it.
glossary.land reclamation: Making usable land by filling water or changing a shore or landscape.
glossary.tax incidence: Who actually bears the cost of a tax, which may not be the person who sends the payment.
glossary.YIMBY: Yes In My Back Yard: someone who supports building more housing in their area.
glossary.fab: A factory where chips are made.
glossary.lithography: A way of using light to print tiny circuit patterns onto silicon when making chips.
glossary.EUV: Extreme Ultraviolet: a kind of light chipmaking machines use to make very small circuit patterns.
glossary.sandbox: A separate, contained space where software can be tested without affecting the rest of a computer or system.
glossary.microVM: A small, separate computer environment for running a job; here, it gets thrown away when the job ends.
glossary.SDK: Software Development Kit: tools a company provides so people can make apps for its device.
glossary.agentic training: Training where an AI practices using tools and taking steps to complete tasks.
glossary.RL: Reinforcement Learning: a way to teach an AI by rewarding actions that get the desired result.
glossary.rollout: A run where an AI tries a task and its actions are recorded for training.
glossary.distributed filesystem: A way to keep files on many computers but use them as one shared file store.
glossary.reward hacking: When an AI finds a way to get a high score without doing what its designers actually wanted.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.agent: An AI system that can take steps and use tools to get a task done, not just answer questions.
glossary.tokens: Small pieces of text an AI counts as it reads or writes; they can affect how much a request costs.
glossary.automated review cycle: A second automated checker looks for problems in a plan or code before a person reviews it.
glossary.Haskell: A programming language the author uses to build software and enjoys writing.
glossary.NAEP: National Assessment of Educational Progress: a US program that checks what students know in subjects such as reading and math.
glossary.PISA: Programme for International Student Assessment: a test program that compares students’ skills across countries.
glossary.OECD: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development: a group of countries that works together on shared economic and social issues.
glossary.PIRLS: Progress in International Reading Literacy Study: a study that checks how well students read.
glossary.ICILS: International Computer and Information Literacy Study: a study of how well students use computers and find information.
glossary.re-weighting: Changing how much different groups count so old results reflect a newer mix of people.
glossary.whole word reading: A way to teach reading by having children recognize entire words instead of sounding them out letter by letter.
glossary.demographics: The makeup of a group, such as how many people belong to different age or background groups.
glossary.emulator: A program that imitates another service so you can try your software without using the real one.
glossary.CLI: Command-Line Interface: a way to control a computer by typing commands instead of clicking buttons.
glossary.cold start: The extra wait while a service starts up after sitting unused.
glossary.integration test: A test that checks whether different parts of a program work together.
glossary.AWS: Amazon Web Services: a collection of cloud services run by Amazon.
glossary.GCP: Google Cloud Platform: Google's collection of cloud services.
glossary.OCI: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure: Oracle's collection of cloud services.
glossary.MIT license: A software license that lets people use, change, and share a project with few restrictions.
glossary.TA: Teaching assistant: someone who helps teach a course and answer students’ questions.
glossary.flipped classroom: A class where students study before meeting, then use class time to discuss or work through problems.
glossary.low-stakes assessment: A quiz or assignment where the result matters less than on a major exam.
glossary.Object Pascal: A form of Pascal that lets programs group related data and actions into reusable parts.
glossary.generics: A way to make one piece of code work with different kinds of values.
glossary.IDE: Integrated Development Environment: an app that brings coding and other development tools together.
glossary.native code: Code compiled into instructions a computer can run directly.
glossary.reference counting: A program tracks how many places share a value so it can manage that value as those places change.
glossary.copy on write: A shared value is copied only when one of the places using it changes it.
glossary.LibGen: A source of books that the filings say OpenAI used to train its systems.
glossary.optics: How an action looks to other people, especially if it could make someone look bad.
glossary.mass piracy: Copying lots of books without permission.
glossary.goroutine: A function Go starts to run alongside other work.
glossary.channel: A way for separate pieces of Go code to send values to one another.
glossary.pipeline: A series of steps where each step works on data and passes it to the next.
glossary.context: A value passed along with work so it can carry a stop signal or a timeout.
glossary.data race: When multiple pieces of work use the same data and at least one changes it.
glossary.race condition: When the order of events can cause a program to end up in the wrong state.
glossary.race detector: A Go tool that checks whether a program has data races.
glossary.mutex: A lock that makes sure only one piece of work at a time uses protected code.
glossary.semaphore: A set of slots that limits how many pieces of work can happen at once.
glossary.select: A Go statement that checks which channel actions are ready, then runs one; if none are ready, it can wait.
glossary.wait group: A counter that keeps track of unfinished work so a program can wait for it to finish.
glossary.classifier: A program that sorts something into a category, such as deciding whether a message is spam.
glossary.disinformation: False or misleading claims spread deliberately to deceive people.
glossary.Balkanisation: A breakup into separate parts; here, it means countries or regions ending up with separate online systems.
glossary.spherical geometry: A way to measure things that accounts for Earth's curved surface.
glossary.IRC: Internet Relay Chat: a way to chat live with people in online rooms.
glossary.public domain: Material people can use without asking a copyright holder for permission.
glossary.found footage: Existing film clips reused to make something new.
glossary.open source: Software whose code is shared so other people can inspect, run, or change it.
glossary.indexing pipeline: A set of steps that labels and organizes material so people can search it.
glossary.pagination: Splitting a long list of results across separate pages.
glossary.permanent residency: Permission to live in a country indefinitely, rather than renewing a temporary visa.
glossary.retroactively: Applied to cases from before a new rule took effect.
glossary.pension pot: Money set aside to provide income after someone retires.
glossary.dual nationality: Being legally recognized as a citizen of two countries at once.
glossary.rightward shift: A move toward more conservative political positions.
glossary.ACP: Agent Client Protocol: a shared way for an AI agent and an app to talk to each other.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI apps to connect to outside tools.
glossary.M365: Microsoft 365: Microsoft's bundle of work apps and services.
glossary.agent orchestration layer: Software that coordinates automated AI helpers and the tools they use to get work done.
glossary.frontier providers: Companies making the most advanced AI systems at a given time.
glossary.OEMs: Original Equipment Manufacturers: companies that make computers or other devices, sometimes sold under another brand's name.
